concepts.name: Vector field
concepts.statement: A vector field F in ℝ² is an assignment of a two-dimensional vector F(x, y) to each point (x, y) of a subset D of ℝ², the domain of the vector field; a vector field in ℝ³ assigns a three-dimensional vector F(x, y, z) to each point (x, y, z) of a subset D of ℝ³. It is written with component functions, F(x, y) = ⟨P(x, y), Q(x, y)⟩ = P i + Q j, or F(x, y, z) = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ = P i + Q j + R k, and it is continuous if its component functions are continuous.

concepts.name: Radial field
concepts.statement: In a radial field, all vectors either point directly toward or directly away from the origin, and the magnitude of any vector depends only on its distance from the origin; the vector at (x, y) is perpendicular to the circle centered at the origin through (x, y).

concepts.name: Rotational field
concepts.statement: In a rotational field, the vector at point (x, y) is tangent to the circle with radius r = √(x² + y²); in a standard rotational field all vectors point clockwise or all counterclockwise, and the magnitude of a vector depends only on its distance from the origin.

concepts.name: Unit vector field
concepts.statement: A vector field F is a unit vector field if the magnitude of each vector in the field is 1; dividing F by its magnitude to form the unit vector field F/‖F‖ = ⟨P/‖F‖, Q/‖F‖, R/‖F‖⟩ is called normalizing F.

concepts.name: Conservative vector field
concepts.statement: A vector field F in ℝ² or in ℝ³ is a gradient field, or conservative field, if there exists a scalar function f such that ∇f = F; such fields model physical systems in which energy is conserved.

concepts.name: Potential function
concepts.statement: If F is a conservative vector field, a scalar function f such that ∇f = F is called a potential function for F.

concepts.name: Uniqueness of potential functions
concepts.statement: Let F be a conservative vector field on an open and connected domain and let f and g be functions such that ∇f = F and ∇g = F. Then there is a constant C such that f = g + C.

concepts.name: Cross-partial property of conservative vector fields
concepts.statement: Let F be a vector field whose component functions have continuous first-order partial derivatives. If F = ⟨P, Q⟩ is conservative in ℝ², then ∂P/∂y = ∂Q/∂x; if F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ is conservative in ℝ³, then ∂P/∂y = ∂Q/∂x, ∂Q/∂z = ∂R/∂y and ∂R/∂x = ∂P/∂z. The converse does not follow, so the property shows a field is not conservative but cannot show that it is.

forms.latex: \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x},\;\frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}=\frac{\partial R}{\partial y},\;\frac{\partial R}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial P}{\partial z}

concepts.name: Line integral
concepts.statement: A line integral is the integral of a function along a curve in a plane or in space: a scalar line integral integrates a scalar function, and a vector line integral a vector field.

concepts.name: Scalar line integral
concepts.statement: Let f be a function with a domain that includes the smooth curve C parameterized by r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b. Chop C into n pieces of lengths Δsᵢ and choose a point Pᵢ* in each; the scalar line integral of f along C is the limit of the sums Σ f(Pᵢ*) Δsᵢ as n → ∞, if it exists. If f ≥ 0, it is the area of the sheet dropped from the curve on the graph of f down to C, and it does not depend on the parameterization.

concepts.name: Scalar line integral calculation
concepts.statement: Let f be a continuous function with a domain that includes the smooth curve C with parameterization r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t), z(t)⟩, a ≤ t ≤ b. Then ∫_C f ds = ∫ₐᵇ f(r(t)) ‖r′(t)‖ dt, so ds = ‖r′(t)‖ dt.

concepts.name: Arc length as a line integral
concepts.statement: If f(x, y, z) = 1, the scalar line integral ∫_C 1 ds is the arc length of C.

concepts.name: Orientation of a curve
concepts.statement: An orientation of a curve C is a specified direction along it, its positive direction, the opposite being the negative direction; an oriented curve is a curve with an orientation, and −C is the same curve with the opposite orientation.

concepts.name: Closed curve
concepts.statement: A closed curve is one for which there exists a parameterization r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, such that r(a) = r(b) and the curve is traversed exactly once: it begins and ends at the same point.

concepts.name: Vector line integral
concepts.statement: The vector line integral of a vector field F along an oriented smooth curve C is the integral of the dot product of F with the unit tangent vector T of C with respect to arc length, the limit of the sums Σ F(Pᵢ*) · T(Pᵢ*) Δsᵢ, if it exists; it is written ∫_C F · dr and is computed from a parameterization as ∫ₐᵇ F(r(t)) · r′(t) dt, or in the form ∫_C P dx + Q dy + R dz.

concepts.name: Work done by a force field
concepts.statement: The work done by a force field F in moving a particle in the positive direction along an oriented curve C is the vector line integral W = ∫_C F · T ds.

concepts.name: Piecewise smooth curve
concepts.statement: A piecewise smooth curve is an oriented curve that is not smooth but can be written as the union C = C₁ + C₂ + ⋯ + Cₙ of finitely many smooth curves, the endpoint of each the starting point of the next.

concepts.name: Properties of vector line integrals
concepts.statement: For continuous vector fields F and G whose domains include the oriented smooth curve C and a constant k: the line integral of F + G is the sum of the line integrals; ∫_C kF · dr = k ∫_C F · dr; reversing the orientation changes the sign, ∫_{−C} F · dr = −∫_C F · dr; and over a piecewise smooth curve C = C₁ + ⋯ + Cₙ the line integral is the sum of the line integrals over the pieces.

concepts.name: Mass of a wire
concepts.statement: If a thin wire has the shape of a curve C and density ρ(x, y, z) per unit length, its mass is the scalar line integral m = ∫_C ρ(x, y, z) ds.

concepts.name: Flux across a curve
concepts.statement: The flux of a vector field F across a plane curve C, the rate at which a fluid flows across C, is the line integral ∫_C F · (n(t)/‖n(t)‖) ds of the normal component of F; for r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t)⟩, a ≤ t ≤ b, and n(t) = ⟨y′(t), −x′(t)⟩ it is ∫_C F · N ds = ∫ₐᵇ F(r(t)) · n(t) dt.

concepts.name: Circulation
concepts.statement: The circulation of a vector field F along an oriented closed curve C is the line integral ∮_C F · T ds, the tendency of a fluid to move in the direction of C.

concepts.name: Simple curve
concepts.statement: A curve C is simple if it does not cross itself: there is a parameterization r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, that is one-to-one over (a, b). A simple curve may also be closed, with r(a) = r(b).

concepts.name: Connected region
concepts.statement: A region D is connected if, for any two points P₁ and P₂ in it, there is a path from P₁ to P₂ with a trace contained entirely inside D.

concepts.name: Simply connected region
concepts.statement: A region D is simply connected if it is connected and any simple closed curve C inside D can be shrunk continuously to a point while staying entirely inside D; in two dimensions, a connected region with no holes.

concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals
concepts.statement: Let C be a piecewise smooth curve with parameterization r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b, and let f be a function of two or three variables with continuous first-order partial derivatives on C. Then the line integral of ∇f along C depends only on the values of f at the endpoints: ∫_C ∇f · dr = f(r(b)) − f(r(a)).

concepts.name: Path independence
concepts.statement: A vector field F with domain D is independent of path (path independent) if ∫_{C₁} F · dr = ∫_{C₂} F · dr for any paths C₁ and C₂ in D with the same initial and terminal points.

concepts.name: Path independence of conservative fields
concepts.statement: If F is a conservative vector field, then F is independent of path; in particular the circulation of a conservative field around any closed curve is zero.

concepts.name: Path independence test for conservative fields
concepts.statement: If F is a continuous vector field that is independent of path and the domain D of F is open and connected, then F is conservative.

concepts.name: Finding a potential function
concepts.statement: To find a potential function for a conservative field F = ⟨P, Q⟩: integrate P with respect to x to get g(x, y) + h(y) with h unknown; take the partial derivative with respect to y; use g_y(x, y) + h′(y) = Q(x, y) to find h′(y); integrate h′(y) to find h(y); then f(x, y) = g(x, y) + h(y) + C for any constant C. In space the same steps add one more unknown function.

concepts.name: Cross-partial test for conservative fields
concepts.statement: If F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ is a vector field on an open, simply connected region D, then P_y = Q_x, P_z = R_x and Q_z = R_y throughout D if and only if F is conservative (in two dimensions, P_y = Q_x).

concepts.name: Green's theorem, circulation form
concepts.statement: Green's theorem relates an integral over a region to an integral over its boundary. Let D be an open, simply connected region whose boundary C is a piecewise smooth, simple closed curve oriented counterclockwise, and let F = ⟨P, Q⟩ have component functions with continuous partial derivatives on D. Then the circulation of F around C equals the double integral of Q_x − P_y over D.

concepts.name: Area by Green's theorem
concepts.statement: If D is a region whose boundary is a simple closed curve C oriented counterclockwise, Green's theorem with F = ⟨−y/2, x/2⟩ gives its area as a line integral around its boundary: area of D = ½ ∮_C −y dx + x dy.

concepts.name: Green's theorem, flux form
concepts.statement: Let D be an open, simply connected region whose boundary C is a piecewise smooth, simple closed curve oriented counterclockwise, and let F = ⟨P, Q⟩ have component functions with continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing D. Then the flux of F across C equals the double integral of P_x + Q_y over D.

concepts.name: Source-free vector field
concepts.statement: A vector field F = ⟨P, Q⟩ on a simply connected domain is source free when any one of these equivalent statements holds: the flux of F across any closed curve is zero; flux is independent of path; F has a stream function; P_x + Q_y = 0.

concepts.name: Stream function
concepts.statement: A stream function for a source-free vector field F = ⟨P, Q⟩ is a function g such that P = g_y and Q = −g_x; F is tangent to the level curves of g, so F · ∇g = 0. Stream functions play the same role for source-free fields that potential functions play for conservative fields.

concepts.name: Harmonic function
concepts.statement: A function f is harmonic if it satisfies Laplace's equation, f_xx + f_yy = 0 (f_xx + f_yy + f_zz = 0 in three variables). A potential function of a vector field that is conservative and source free on a simply connected domain is harmonic.

concepts.name: Green's theorem on general regions
concepts.statement: Green's theorem extends to a region D with finitely many holes: cut D into simply connected pieces, whose line integrals over the common boundaries cancel, and the circulation of F around the oriented boundary ∂D of D equals ∬_D (Q_x − P_y) dA; the flux form extends the same way.

concepts.name: Divergence
concepts.statement: If F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ is a vector field in ℝ³ and P_x, Q_y and R_z all exist, the divergence of F is the scalar function div F = ∇ · F = P_x + Q_y + R_z (in ℝ², P_x + Q_y). It measures the tendency of the fluid to flow out of a point: positive where the point is a source, negative where it is a sink.

forms.latex: \operatorname{div}\mathbf{F}=P_{x}+Q_{y}+R_{z}=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}

concepts.name: Divergence test for source-free vector fields
concepts.statement: If F = ⟨P, Q⟩ is a source-free continuous vector field with differentiable component functions, then div F = 0; on a simply connected domain the converse holds too, so div F = 0 if and only if F is source free.

concepts.name: Curl
concepts.statement: If F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ is a vector field in ℝ³ whose first partial derivatives all exist, the curl of F is the vector field curl F = ∇ × F = (R_y − Q_z) i + (P_z − R_x) j + (Q_x − P_y) k, the “determinant” of the matrix with rows i, j, k; ∂/∂x, ∂/∂y, ∂/∂z; and P, Q, R. It measures the tendency of particles at a point to rotate about the axis that points in its direction, as a small paddlewheel would.

concepts.name: Divergence of the curl
concepts.statement: If F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ is a vector field in ℝ³ whose component functions have continuous second-order partial derivatives, then div curl F = ∇ · (∇ × F) = 0.

concepts.name: Curl of a conservative vector field
concepts.statement: If F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ is conservative, then curl F = 0: the curl of a gradient is the zero vector.

concepts.name: Curl test for a conservative field
concepts.statement: Let F = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ be a vector field in space on a simply connected domain. If curl F = 0, then F is conservative.

concepts.name: Laplace operator
concepts.statement: The divergence of a gradient, div(∇f) = ∇ · (∇f) = f_xx + f_yy + f_zz, is written ∇²f; ∇² is the Laplace operator, and Laplace's equation becomes ∇²f = 0, so a harmonic function is one whose divergence of its gradient is zero.

concepts.name: Parametric surface
concepts.statement: A parameterized (or parametric) surface is a surface given by a description r(u, v) = ⟨x(u, v), y(u, v), z(u, v)⟩, where the parameters u and v vary over a region of the uv-plane.

concepts.name: Parameter domain
concepts.statement: The parameter domain, or parameter space, of a parameterization r(u, v) of a surface is the set of points in the uv-plane that can be substituted into r.

concepts.name: Regular parameterization
concepts.statement: A parameterization r(u, v) is regular, or smooth, if r_u × r_v is not zero for any point (u, v) in the parameter domain; a surface with a regular parameterization is smooth, and one made of finitely many smooth pieces is piecewise smooth.

concepts.name: Grid curves
concepts.statement: The images under r(u, v) of the grid lines u = constant and v = constant of the parameter domain are the grid curves of the surface, curves on the surface parallel to grid lines in a coordinate plane; their tangent vectors are t_u = r_u and t_v = r_v, and where t_u × t_v ≠ 0 they span the tangent plane.

forms.latex: \mathbf{t}_{u}=\left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial u},\frac{\partial y}{\partial u},\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\right\rangle,\;\mathbf{t}_{v}=\left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial v},\frac{\partial y}{\partial v},\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\right\rangle

concepts.name: Surface area of a parametric surface
concepts.statement: Let r(u, v) with parameter domain D be a smooth parameterization of a surface S traced out once. The surface area of S is ∬_D ‖t_u × t_v‖ dA, the limit of the sums of the areas ‖t_u × t_v‖ Δu Δv of the parallelograms that approximate its pieces; it equals the surface integral ∬_S dS.

concepts.name: Surface integral
concepts.statement: A surface integral is an integral of a function over a surface: of a scalar function, or of a vector field across an oriented surface.

concepts.name: Surface integral of a scalar-valued function
terms: surface integral of a scalar-valued function
concepts.statement: The surface integral of a scalar function f over a piecewise smooth surface S is the limit of the sums ΣΣ f(P_ij) ΔS_ij over pieces S_ij of area ΔS_ij; for a smooth parameterization r(u, v) over D it is ∬_D f(r(u, v)) ‖t_u × t_v‖ dA.

concepts.name: Orientation of a surface
concepts.statement: A surface is orientable if it has an “inner” side and an “outer” side; an orientation is a choice of unit normal vector N at each point that varies continuously, pointing to one side. A closed surface is positively oriented when N points outward; the Möbius strip has only one side and cannot be oriented.

concepts.name: Surface integral of a vector field
terms: surface integral of a vector field
concepts.statement: Let F be a continuous vector field with a domain that contains the oriented surface S with unit normal vector N. The surface integral of F over S, or flux integral, is ∬_S F · dS = ∬_S F · N dS, the flux of F across S; for a parameterization r(u, v) over D it is ∬_D F(r(u, v)) · (t_u × t_v) dA.

concepts.name: Mass flux
concepts.statement: The mass flux of a fluid of density ρ and velocity field v is the rate of mass flow per unit area; the mass of fluid flowing across a surface S per unit time is the flux integral ∬_S ρv · N dS.

concepts.name: Heat flow
concepts.statement: If T(x, y, z) is the temperature in an object, the heat flow is the vector field F = −k∇T, proportional to the negative temperature gradient, where k is the object's thermal conductivity; the rate of heat flow across a surface S is its flux ∬_S −k∇T · dS.

concepts.name: Stokes' theorem
concepts.statement: Let S be a piecewise smooth oriented surface whose boundary is a simple closed curve C with positive orientation, and let F have component functions with continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing S. Then the line integral of F around C equals the flux of curl F across S.

concepts.name: Surface independence of flux integrals of curl fields
concepts.statement: If S₁ and S₂ are two surfaces with the same boundary curve C, oriented compatibly, then by Stokes' theorem ∬_{S₁} curl F · dS = ∮_C F · dr = ∬_{S₂} curl F · dS: flux integrals of curl fields are surface independent, as line integrals of gradient fields are path independent.

concepts.name: Curl as circulation per unit area
concepts.statement: If D_r is a small disk of radius r centered at P with normal N and boundary C_r, then curl F(P) · N = lim_{r→0} (1/(πr²)) ∮_{C_r} F · dr: the component of curl F along N is the circulation of F per unit area about N, the spin a small paddlewheel at P with its axis along N would show.

concepts.name: Faraday's law
concepts.statement: Faraday's law states that a changing magnetic field B induces an electric field E: in integral form, the work done by E around the boundary C of a surface D equals minus the rate of change of the flux of B across D, ∮_C E · dr = −∂Φ/∂t; by Stokes' theorem this is equivalent to the differential form curl E = −∂B/∂t.

concepts.name: Divergence theorem
concepts.statement: Let S be a piecewise smooth closed surface that encloses a solid E in space, oriented outward, and let F have continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing E. Then the triple integral of div F over E equals the flux of F across S.

concepts.name: Divergence as flux per unit volume
concepts.statement: If B_r is a small ball of radius r centered at P with boundary sphere S_r, then div F(P) = lim_{r→0} (1/vol(B_r)) ∬_{S_r} F · dS: the divergence at P is the flux out of P per unit volume, positive at a source and negative at a sink.

concepts.name: Inverse-square law
concepts.statement: The electrostatic field of a point charge q at the origin is E = (q/(4πε₀)) F_r, where F_r = (1/r²)⟨x/r, y/r, z/r⟩; the force at a point is inversely proportional to the square of its distance from the charge, so electrostatic fields obey an inverse-square law.

concepts.name: Flux of the inverse-square field across a closed surface
concepts.statement: Let S be a connected, piecewise smooth closed surface. The flux of F_r = (1/r²)⟨x/r, y/r, z/r⟩ across S is 0 if S does not encompass the origin and 4π if it does, since div F_r = 0 away from the origin.

forms.latex: \iint_{S}\mathbf{F}_{r}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\begin{cases}0&S\text{ does not encompass the origin}\\4\pi&S\text{ encompasses the origin}\end{cases}

concepts.name: Gauss' law
concepts.statement: If S is a piecewise smooth closed surface in a vacuum and Q is the total stationary charge inside S, then the flux of the electrostatic field E across S is Q/ε₀.
